title: Area Routing
description: Learn how to organize large ASP.NET Core applications using Areas. Understand the folder structure, area route patterns, and how Areas help separate features like Admin, Blog, and API into self-contained modules.

blocks.text: As an ASP.NET Core application grows, you may find yourself with dozens of controllers and hundreds of views. **Areas** provide a way to partition a large application into smaller, self-contained functional groups — each with its own controllers, views, and route configuration.
Common uses for areas include separating an **Admin** section from the public-facing site, organizing a multi-tenant application, or isolating a set of related features like **Blog** or **Store**.

An Area is a logical grouping of controllers, views, models, and routes within your application. Each area has its own folder under the main `Areas/` directory, and its own route configuration that includes the area name as a URL segment.

blocks.title: Area folder structure
blocks.content: The folder layout for an application with an Admin area.
blocks.code:
MyFirstApp/
├── Controllers/          # Root-level controllers (HomeController)
├── Views/                 # Root-level views
├── Areas/
│   └── Admin/
│       ├── Controllers/
│       │   └── DashboardController.cs
│       ├── Views/
│       │   └── Dashboard/
│       │       └── Index.cshtml
│       └── AdminAreaRegistration.cs  (optional)
└── Program.cs

blocks.title: Areas are optional
blocks.text: Small to medium applications rarely need areas. Use them when you have a clear functional grouping (admin panel, blog, store) that justifies the extra folder structure. For simple applications, stick with a flat controller structure.

Areas require two things: the controllers must have the `[Area]` attribute, and the routing system must include an area-aware route pattern. The area route uses the `{area:exists}` constraint to match only requests that include an area segment.

blocks.title: Area route configuration
blocks.content: Add area-aware routing to Program.cs and apply the [Area] attribute to controllers.

blocks.text: The `{area:exists}` constraint ensures the route only matches when an area name is present in the URL. The area route must come before the default route because the routing system uses first-match semantics.

With the area route pattern `{area:exists}/{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}`, the URL `/Admin/Dashboard/Index` maps to `AdminArea` → `DashboardController` → `Index()` action. The area name becomes the first URL segment.

blocks.title: URL to area mapping examples
items: `/Products/Details/5` → Root level, ProductsController, Details(5) — no area

blocks.text: Views for area controllers live in `Areas/[AreaName]/Views/[ControllerName]/`. The view lookup follows the same convention as root-level views, but scoped to the area. The default layout is still `Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml` unless you specify a different layout.

blocks.title: Area view with a different layout
blocks.content: Override the default layout for an Admin area view to use an admin-specific layout.

blocks.text: When generating links to actions in a different area, you need to specify the area name in the route values. Failing to do so will generate a link to the same area, which may not exist.

blocks.title: Linking from root to an area action
blocks.content: Use Url.Action with the area route value to generate links to area controllers.
blocks.code: @* Link from a root view to the Admin Dashboard *@ Admin Dashboard @* Link from Admin area back to the home page (root level) *@ Back to Site

blocks.title: Area links in the same area
blocks.text: When linking between two actions within the same area, you do not need to specify the area name — it is implied by the current request. Only specify `area = "..."` when crossing area boundaries.
Areas are an excellent place to apply authorization policies. You can use `[Authorize]` on the entire area controller or individual actions to restrict access to authenticated or admin users.

blocks.title: Securing an entire area
blocks.content: Apply [Authorize] to all controllers in an area by adding it to the controller base class or using a convention.

blocks.title: Good candidates for areas
items: **Admin panel** — Separate admin controllers, views, and authorization from the public site
**Multi-tenant apps** — Each tenant gets its own area with isolated controllers and views
**Large feature modules** — Isolate a complex feature (Blog, Store, Forum) to keep controllers manageable
**API versioning** — Separate v1 and v2 API controllers into different areas for cleaner organization

blocks.title: Do not overuse areas
blocks.text: Areas add complexity. For small applications with a handful of controllers, a flat structure is simpler and easier to navigate. Introduce areas only when the folder structure becomes genuinely hard to manage.

terms.definition: A functional grouping within an ASP.NET Core application with its own controllers, views, and route configuration. Areas help organize large applications.
A route pattern that includes the area segment (e.g., {area:exists}/{controller}/{action}) to match URLs that target a specific area.
The [Area("AreaName")] attribute applied to controllers to specify which area they belong to.
A route constraint that matches only when an area name is present in the URL. Used to distinguish area routes from root-level routes.

items.text: I have created an Areas/[AreaName] folder structure with Controllers and Views subfolders
I have applied [Area("AreaName")] to controllers in the area
I have added the area route pattern {area:exists}/{controller}/{action}/{id?} before the default route
items.hint: Area routes must come BEFORE the default route in Program.cs

items.text: I can generate a link from a root view to an area action
I understand when areas are appropriate and when a flat structure is better
items.hint: Use areas for Admin panels, multi-tenant apps, or large feature modules

blocks.title: Create an Admin Area
blocks.description: Organize your application by creating an Admin area with its own controllers, views, and route configuration.
steps: Create `DashboardController.cs` in the Admin Controllers folder with [Area("Admin")] attribute
Add an `Index()` action that returns a simple view with an Admin heading
Create `Index.cshtml` in the Admin Views/Dashboard folder with admin page content
Update Program.cs to add the area route `{area:exists}/{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}` BEFORE the default route
Run the app and visit `/Admin/Dashboard` to confirm the Admin area loads
Add a link in the root Home page that points to the Admin Dashboard using `Url.Action("Index", "Dashboard", new { area = "Admin" })`
blocks.expectedOutcome: Visiting `/Admin/Dashboard` renders the Admin area's Dashboard/Index view. The link from the root Home page correctly navigates to the Admin Dashboard. The Admin area is visually or functionally distinct from the root application.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Areas partition a large application into self-contained functional groups with their own controllers and views
Enable areas with `{area:exists}/{controller}/{action}/{id?}` in Program.cs, before the default route
Apply [Area("AreaName")] to controllers to assign them to a specific area
Area views live in `Areas/[AreaName]/Views/[Controller]/` following the same convention as root views
Cross-area links require specifying the area name: `Url.Action("Action", "Controller", new { area = "AreaName" })`
Use areas for Admin panels, multi-tenant apps, and large feature modules — not for small applications
blocks.takeaway: Areas provide a clean organizational structure for large ASP.NET Core applications. By separating features into isolated modules with their own controllers, views, and routes, areas keep your codebase manageable as it grows.
